https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/.text: A third drone has been shot down by Romanian forces in just three days, Romanian President Nicușor Dan has announced, adding to a string of drone-related incidents in the country.In a statement on social media, Dan said a Romanian air force F-16 fighter jet had intercepted a drone over Romania's territorial waters at around 10:13 am on Sunday morning. The incident reportedly occurred in the Sulina–Chilia area of the Danube Delta, close to the border with Ukraine."I would like to congratulate the Romanian pilots and ground crews on the professionalism, courage and efficiency with which they carry out their missions," Dan wrote on X.Romanian authorities reported that an F-16 shot down another unmanned aerial vehicle on Saturday morning, roughly 10 km west of the village of Sfântu Gheorghe in eastern Romania.Two jets were scrambled to identify and intercept the target, and the drone was "safely shot down in an unpopulated area near the border," the Romanian Defence Ministry said in a statement on Saturday.A third drone was shot down by a Romanian F-16 at around 11 am on Friday.The Romanian Prosecutor General's Office has determined that the drone intercepted on Friday was of the Shahed-type used by Russian forces in its war against Ukraine, Romanian officials have said.While investigations into the drones shot down on Saturday and Sunday are still ongoing, Dan said it was "intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace.""Such actions are unacceptable and we are treating them with the utmost seriousness, alongside our allies," he added.Romania's growing drone problemSituated on NATO's eastern flank and on the shores of the Black Sea, Romania is particularly vulnerable to security challenges arising from Russia's war against Ukraine, which began after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022.Bucharest has seen a surge in drone-related incidents and incursions into Romanian airspace in recent months, prompting officials to pledge heightened security measures across the country.In May, a Russian drone carrying explosives crashed into an apartment block in Galați, sparking a fire on the roof and injuring two people.The following month, a Ukrainian sea drone also exploded in the Romanian port of Constanta. The Ukrainian military said it had veered off course as a result of Russian electronic warfare interference.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has labelled such incidents "a direct consequence of Russia’s war against Ukraine."

A communications conference in Rome in 2027 will explore how Catholic journalists and media professionals can help foster a climate of trust. The convocation for "Nurturing Unity Through Communication" will be hosted by the Pontifical University of the Holy Cross in Rome from Feb. 2–4, 2027. Typically held every two years, it will be the 15th edition of the Professional Seminar for Church Communications Offices. The event is being organized in collaboration with the Vatican's Dicastery for Communication and is expected to draw over 500 participants, including Catholic communications professionals from dioceses, religious orders, and episcopal conferences. Conference sponsors also include EWTN News, Rome Reports, and the Pontifical Mission Societies. According to the event website, the gathering will invite participants to reflect "on the role of institutional communication as a path toward fostering unity and concord both within and beyond the Church." The seminar is also inspired by Pope Leo XIV's call for Catholic media professionals to strive for peace in their work. "Addressing communicators in his first public audience as pope, Leo XIV reminded them: 'Peace begins with each one of us: with the way we look at others, listen to others, speak about others; and, in this sense, the way we communicate is of fundamental importance: We must say 'no' to the war of words and images; we must reject the paradigm of war.'" The conference will include plenary and parallel sessions covering topics ranging from social media to encouraging diversity rather than promoting division in the Church through media. EWTN Chairman and CEO Michael Warsaw will speak on the topic "Leading Through Digital Disruption: Building Community in a Changing Media Landscape." EWTN Vice President and Chief Global Officer Andreas Thonhauser, meanwhile, will moderate a discussion of "AI and Magnifica Humanitas : Reflections One Year On." Registration for the conference is open until Dec. 1 and can be made through the Pontifical University of the Holy Cross by clicking here . https://www.dw.com/en/saudi-arabia-suspe.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5O76U Major airlines have suspended operations in Riyadh amid security threats [FILE: February 15, 2023] Image: Markus Mainka/picture alliance Advertisement A number of people were injured in an attack on Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia on Saturday, the country's civil aviation authority has confirmed. "King Khalid International Airport was targeted by an attack, amid continued attacks targeting civilian aviation facilities in the kingdom," the General Authority of Civil Aviation said in a statement. "The attack resulted in a number of injures, which are currently being assessed." The General Authority of Civil Aviation said operations at the airport had been suspended until further notice. What do we know about the attack? A Saudi official, speaking on the condition of anonymity, told the Associated Press that many people were wounded after a missile hit a passenger terminal. The AFP news news agency also reported that a number of people were injured, citing a local medical source who also spoke on the condition of anonymity. "ER doctors are being called to hospitals across Riyadh," the source told AFP. "We were told we are dealing with a 'serious emergency situation'. Injured are being moved to hospitals across Riyadh." Several Western embassies in Riyadh, including those of Germany, the United States, Canada and Spain, urged citizens to avoid the airport. The US embassy said it was "aware of attacks" at the airport. Spain's embassy referred to a "new attack" by the Houthi rebels in Yemen while Canada's embassy warned of "ongoing military activity." When asked about the attack, US President Donald Trump said the US would soon decide whether to join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthis in Yemen. "We may. We're going to look at it. We just found out about the recent attack, so we'll make a decision," Trump told reporters at the White House. "We move very quickly." Strikes hit Riyadh airport earlier this week The reports come amid intensified fighting between Houthi rebels and the Saudi-backed government in Yemen. The Iran-backed Houthis have been launching strikes on targets in Saudi Arabia, including several this week on the airport in Riyadh that killed four people, injured several others, and damaged planes. Etihad Airways and Qatar Airways canceled multiple flights between their ​respective hubs and Riyadh, with some cancellations extending into Monday. Kuwait Airways also cancelled its flights on Saturday. King Khalid Airport was hit earlier this week in an attack claimed by Yemen-based Houthi rebels Image: Social Media/REUTERS There was no immediate Houthi statement about the reported blast on Saturday. Last month, Houthi rebels made advances on important strategic locations along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with a Saudi-led coalition providing air support for Yemeni government forces seeking to take back those gains. The Houthis have responded by launching attacks into Saudi Arabia, which represents a significant escalation in their multi-year conflict with Yemen's Riyadh-backed government after a peace deal unraveled in July. The Saudi-backed government in Yemen last week announced a counter-offensive aimed at retaking all areas held by the Houthis, especially those around the Bab al-Mandab strait. Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis?
